what_its_for: Estradiol cypionate is a form of estrogen, a female hormone. It is used to treat symptoms of menopause such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. It may also be used for conditions where the body does not make enough estrogen, such as when the ovaries have been removed or do not work properly. In some cases, it is used as part of hormone therapy for transgender women.
how_to_take: This medication is given as a shot (injection) into a muscle, usually in the buttock or upper arm. A healthcare provider will typically give you this injection in a clinic or doctor's office. If you are taught to give yourself injections at home, follow the exact instructions your healthcare provider shows you. Always use a new, sterile needle and syringe each time. Do not inject into a vein. Rotate injection sites to avoid soreness or skin changes in one area.
dosing: The dose and how often you get the injection depends on your condition and what your doctor decides is right for you. For menopause symptoms, a common dose is 1 to 5 mg injected into the muscle every 3 to 4 weeks. For hormone therapy in transgender women, doses may vary and are adjusted based on your hormone levels and response to treatment. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never change your dose without talking to them first.
missed_dose: If you miss a scheduled injection, contact your healthcare provider or clinic as soon as possible to reschedule. Do not try to give yourself a double dose to make up for the missed one. Your doctor may adjust your schedule if needed. Try to keep all your injection appointments to get the most benefit from this medication.
storage: Store estradiol cypionate at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from light, heat, and moisture. Do not freeze it. Keep this medication out of reach of children and pets. If you notice the solution looks cloudy, has particles in it, or has changed color, do not use it and ask your pharmacist for a replacement. Dispose of used needles and syringes safely in a puncture-resistant sharps container.
what_to_avoid: Avoid smoking while using estrogen therapy, as smoking greatly increases the risk of serious side effects such as blood clots, stroke, and heart attack, especially if you are over 35 years old. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice as it may increase the amount of estrogen in your blood. Tell your doctor about all other medications, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take, especially blood thinners, thyroid medications, or St. John's Wort, as they can interact with estradiol. Avoid prolonged sitting or lying down on long trips, as estrogen can increase clotting risk.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have any of these warning signs: sudden chest pain or tightness, trouble breathing or shortness of breath, sudden severe headache, vision changes or sudden loss of vision, pain or swelling in your legs (possible blood clot), weakness or numbness on one side of your body, or sudden confusion or trouble speaking. Also call your doctor if you notice unusual vaginal bleeding, yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice), breast lumps, mood changes or depression, or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: You may start to notice some improvement in hot flashes and other menopause symptoms within a few weeks of starting treatment. However, it may take 1 to 3 months of regular injections to feel the full benefit. Vaginal dryness and other physical changes may take a bit longer to improve. For transgender hormone therapy, physical changes such as breast development and skin softening happen gradually and may take several months to years to fully develop. Be patient and keep all your follow-up appointments so your doctor can check your hormone levels and adjust your dose if needed.
special_populations: Older adults (over 65): Use with caution. Older women may have a higher risk of serious side effects including dementia, blood clots, stroke, and breast cancer with long-term estrogen use. The lowest effective dose for the shortest time needed is recommended. Pregnant individuals: Do not use estradiol cypionate if you are pregnant or think you might be pregnant. It can cause harm to an unborn baby. Breastfeeding: Estrogen can pass into breast milk and may reduce milk supply. Talk to your doctor before using this medication if you are breastfeeding. Teens and children: This medication is not typically recommended for use in children who have not yet gone through puberty unless prescribed by a specialist for a specific medical condition. People with certain health conditions: Tell your doctor if you have a history of blood clots, stroke, heart disease, liver disease, breast cancer, uterine cancer, migraines, high blood pressure, diabetes, or high triglycerides, as these conditions may affect whether this medication is safe for you.
